1072.title: Last words
1072.hook: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah enters the garden (Abu Dawud)
1072.carry: let these be my last words
1072.howItsDone: Muslims at a deathbed often say la ilaha illallah softly near the dying person, a practice called talqin, and some say the shahada or the bedtime supplication taught in the hadith as the last words before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shia adhan: the call, as each hears it. Today, the testimony's last word.

A room late at night, the lamp turned low. An old woman in the bed, her breathing slow and uneven. Her son sits close and, every so often, without any pressure in his voice, says a few words near her ear: la ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. He isn't quizzing her. He's leaving the words in the air, the way you'd leave a light on in the hallway, in case she wants to reach for them. Then he goes quiet again, and the room holds the words with him.
screen: `A LAMP TURNED LOW.` → `A FEW WORDS, NEAR HER EAR.` → `A LIGHT LEFT ON IN THE HALLWAY.`

segments.voice: The son is following two sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The first is in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 3116: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter the garden. The second is in Sahih Muslim, number 916: prompt your dying with la ilaha illallah. The word for that gentle prompting is talqin. Scholars who explain it advise doing it softly, saying the words rather than ordering the dying person to repeat them, and not pressing if they've already said them. An open door, not a test. Now turn it around. Nobody chooses the hour. So how does anyone make sure of their last words? Sahih al-Bukhari, number 247, gives one answer. The Prophet ﷺ told a companion: when you go to bed, make wudu as for prayer, lie on your right side, and say a short supplication handing yourself over to God. If you die that night, he said, you die on the natural way, and he told him to make those words the last thing he said. So bedtime becomes a rehearsal. Sleep, in this teaching, is a small cousin of death; the Qur'an, at 39:42, speaks of God taking souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died, in their sleep. Some Muslims join these teachings and say the shahada as the very last thing before sleep, night after night, so the words are well worn by the time they're needed.
screen: `PROMPT YOUR DYING, SOFTLY.` · `AN OPEN DOOR, NOT A TEST.` · `NOBODY CHOOSES THE HOUR.` · `BEDTIME AS A REHEARSAL.` · then, large: `LA ILAHA ILLALLAH.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie as you might at bedtime, and let the day go out of your shoulders. If you're Muslim and you pray, say la ilaha illallah slowly, once, and let the quiet hold it; if not, sit with the question the son was answering: what words do I want close by at the end? If this brings up grief or a heaviness that won't lift, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Last words. In this teaching, the shahada said at the end, prompted gently by those who love you, and rehearsed every night before sleep. Today's word.
Your line: let these be my last words. Night after night, the words grow familiar. Tomorrow, the prayer begins.

1073.title: Before the prayer
1073.hook: conditions: being Muslim, sane, of age, clean, covered, facing the qiblah, in time
1073.howItsDone: Before each prayer, Muslims make sure they are in a state of purification, dressed with the required covering, on a clean spot, facing the Ka'ba in Mecca, and within the prayer's time, and only then begin with Allahu akbar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, last words: the testimony at the end, rehearsed each night. Today a new part opens: the prayer.

Gate 23, a delayed flight, and the afternoon prayer time already open. A woman sets down her bag and runs a quiet checklist. Did her wudu survive the security line? She thinks it did. Is her scarf where it should be? Yes. Is the carpet by the window clean enough? She lays a jacket down to be sure. Which way is Mecca from here? Her phone's compass points past the vending machine. How long until the time runs out? Long enough. Only then does she raise her hands and say Allahu akbar. Everything before that moment has a name.
screen: `A DELAYED FLIGHT, AN OPEN PRAYER TIME.` → `A QUIET CHECKLIST.` → `ONLY THEN: ALLAHU AKBAR.`

segments.voice: The name is shurut, conditions. In the fiqh books, they're what must already be true before the prayer starts, before that opening Allahu akbar, the takbir. They sit outside the prayer, like the frame around a door; the standing, bowing and prostrating inside it have a different name, and they come later. Start with the person. The prayer is the act of a Muslim of sound mind who has reached the age of responsibility. A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 4403, says the pen is lifted from three: the sleeper until he wakes, the child until he grows up, and the one who has lost his reason until he recovers. Then the body and the place. Clean: Sahih Muslim, number 224, says a prayer is not accepted without purification. Covered: the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, says, "O Children of Adam! Look to your adornment at every place of worship." The schools spell out what covering means, and they differ in the details. Then direction. The Qur'an tells the Prophet ﷺ, "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship," the Ka'ba in Mecca. Then time. The Qur'an says that "worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." A prayer said before its time has opened hasn't met its condition. Read the list again and it's almost all about arriving: in the right state, at the right moment, facing the right way. Then the prayer itself can be about only one thing.
screen: `CONDITIONS: TRUE BEFORE IT STARTS.` · `THE PERSON: MUSLIM, SANE, OF AGE.` · `CLEAN, COVERED, FACING THE KA'BA.` · `IN ITS TIME.` · then, large: `WORSHIP AT FIXED HOURS.`

segments.voice: Check each one slowly, the way the woman at the gate did: your hands and face, and whether you feel clean; your clothes, and whether you're dressed as you'd want to be before something that matters; your direction, and whether you know where Mecca lies from here; and the time of day. If you pray, you can run this check before your next prayer; if you don't, it works before any moment that matters.
Shurut. Conditions: what must already be true before the prayer begins. The person, clean, covered, facing the qiblah, and in time. Today's word.
Your line: ready before the takbir. The frame goes up before the door opens. Same time tomorrow.

1074.title: Wudu in detail
1074.hook: the required parts: face, arms to elbows, wiping the head, feet, and the sunnah additions
1074.howItsDone: Muslims make wudu before prayer by washing the face, the arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and washing or wiping the feet as their school teaches, usually adding the sunnah steps: hands, mouth, nose and ears, right before left.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shurut, the conditions: ready before the takbir. One of them was being clean. Today, how.

Uthman ibn Affan, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asks for a vessel of water. Humran, who reports the scene, is watching. Uthman doesn't explain. He shows. He pours water over his hands, three times. He dips his right hand in and rinses his mouth and his nose. He washes his face, three times. His arms up to the elbows. He passes his wet hands over his head. He washes his feet up to the ankles. Then he says: I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ make wudu just like this. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene, at number 159.
screen: `A VESSEL OF WATER, SOMEONE WATCHING.` → `HANDS, MOUTH, NOSE, FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` → `I SAW HIM DO IT LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: Year two read the wudu verse; today, the washing itself. Uthman's demonstration holds two layers, and the fiqh books separate them. The first is in the Qur'an, 5:6, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and (wash) your feet up to the ankles." Face, arms, head, feet: the required parts, without which the wudu isn't done. The second layer is everything else Uthman showed: washing the hands first, rinsing the mouth and nose, starting on the right, doing the washings three times. Other reports add wiping the ears. These are the sunnah additions, what the Prophet ﷺ did, and Muslims follow them as part of doing it well. Inside the verse, the schools read some words differently, and they say so openly. How much of the head must be wiped? The schools give different answers. And the feet: Sunni schools read the verse as washing them; Shia jurists read it as wiping them. Each reads the same Arabic carefully and arrives at its own practice. Notice the verse doesn't say be pure in general. It names a face, two arms, a head, two feet. Purity, here, goes limb by limb. And Uthman closed by reporting that whoever makes wudu like this and then prays two units without letting the mind wander has past sins forgiven. The outer water and the inner focus, one movement.
screen: `THE VERSE: FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` · `THE SUNNAH: HANDS, MOUTH, NOSE, EARS.` · `THE SCHOOLS READ SOME WORDS DIFFERENTLY.` · `LIMB BY LIMB, THEN A FOCUSED PRAYER.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR FACES, AND YOUR HANDS UP TO THE ELBOWS.`

segments.voice: If you make wudu and water is near, make it now and name each limb under your breath as you wash it: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, ears, feet. If you don't, follow it where you sit, resting your attention on your hands, then your face, your forearms, the top of your head, your feet. One part at a time, each finished before the next.
Wudu in detail. The required parts from the verse, face, arms, head, feet, and the sunnah around them, as Uthman showed. Today's word.
Your line: each limb washed. A small washing, done with care. Next, what breaks wudu.

1075.title: What breaks wudu
1075.hook: using the toilet, deep sleep, passing wind, and details that differ by school
1075.howItsDone: Muslims renew wudu after using the toilet, passing wind, deep sleep or losing consciousness, and follow their school on the debated cases, such as touching the opposite sex, bleeding, or eating camel meat; a passing doubt does not break it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wudu in detail: each limb washed, the verse and the sunnah around it. Today, how long that washing lasts.

A man from Hadramawt, in the south of Arabia, has heard Abu Hurayrah repeat a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: the prayer of someone in a state of hadath isn't accepted until he makes wudu. Hadath. It's a technical word, and the man doesn't pretend to know it. So he asks, out loud: what is hadath? And Abu Hurayrah gives him a plain answer. Passing wind. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the exchange, at number 135, question and answer together.
screen: `A MAN FROM HADRAMAWT.` → `WHAT IS HADATH?` → `A PLAIN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Wudu isn't a once-a-day stamp. It lasts until something ends it, and the fiqh books call those things nawaqid, the breakers. The schools share a core. Whatever leaves the body by the two private passages: using the toilet, passing wind. Deep sleep, the kind where you lose track of yourself; a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 203, ties sleep to wudu. And losing consciousness. Then come the details, where the schools part ways and say so. Touching the skin of someone of the opposite sex: the Shafi'i school counts it as a breaker, the Hanafi school does not, and the Maliki school looks at whether there was desire. Bleeding from a wound breaks wudu for the Hanafis and not for the Shafi'is. And in Sahih Muslim, number 360, someone asks the Prophet ﷺ whether to make wudu after eating camel meat, and he says yes; the Hanbali school takes that as a breaker, while other schools read it differently. So each school has its own list. Then there's the rule that steadies the whole thing. In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 137, a man tells the Prophet ﷺ he sometimes imagines something has happened during prayer. The answer: don't leave the prayer unless you hear a sound or notice a smell. Scholars turned that into a principle: certainty isn't removed by doubt. Wudu ends for a reason, not a worry. And when it ends, the answer is simple. Wash again.
screen: `WUDU LASTS UNTIL SOMETHING ENDS IT.` · `THE SHARED CORE: TOILET, WIND, DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE SCHOOLS DIFFER ON THE DETAILS.` · `A DOUBT DOESN'T BREAK IT.` · then, large: `CERTAINTY ISN'T REMOVED BY DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Pick one small worry you're carrying right now, the kind the mind invents: did I lock the door, did I say the wrong thing, did that count. Ask it the question from the hadith: did you hear a sound, did you notice a smell, is anything here certain, or only a feeling? If nothing is certain, set it down for now; and if you pray and follow a school, its list of breakers is worth knowing instead of guessing.
What breaks wudu. A shared core, the toilet, wind, deep sleep, details that differ by school, and a doubt that breaks nothing. Today's word.
Your line: renew it. A doubt breaks nothing, and a real reason only means fresh water. Up next: the full bath.

1076.title: The full bath
1076.hook: a full wash after intimacy, after menstruation, before Friday and Eid
1076.howItsDone: Muslims make ghusl, a full-body wash with intention, after intimacy and after menstruation or postnatal bleeding before praying again, and as a recommended bath before the Friday prayer and the Eid prayers, following the steps Aishah described.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what breaks wudu, and a line: renew it. Wudu washes some limbs. Today, the wash that covers everything.

Friday morning, early. The kettle's on, the kids are still asleep, and a father stands in the shower a little longer than usual. He isn't lingering. He's working through an order: hands first, then the wudu he knows by heart, then water through the roots of his hair, then over his head, then over the whole body, right side, left side, until nothing is left dry. Later he'll put on his good shirt and go to the Friday prayer. To anyone passing the bathroom door, it's just a shower. To him it has a name, and steps that come from a description kept in the hadith.
screen: `FRIDAY MORNING, EARLY.` → `A SHOWER WITH AN ORDER.` → `UNTIL NOTHING IS LEFT DRY.`

segments.voice: The name is ghusl, the full bath. Where wudu washes certain limbs, ghusl reaches the whole body. The Qur'an names it in the same verse that gives wudu, 5:6, and Pickthall's translation puts it simply: "And if ye are unclean, purify yourselves." The fiqh books list when ghusl is required: after sexual intimacy, after a woman's menstruation ends, and after the bleeding that follows childbirth. Without it, the prayer waits. Then there are times when it's recommended, a gift rather than a duty. Before the Friday prayer: in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 877, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that whoever comes to the Friday prayer should bathe first. Scholars discuss whether that wording makes it required or strongly recommended. And before the Eid prayers, which reports say companions of the Prophet ﷺ did. Now the steps. In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 248, Aishah describes how he bathed. He began by washing his hands. Then he made wudu as for prayer. Then he ran his fingers through the roots of his hair, poured three handfuls of water over his head, and let water flow over his whole body. That's the full sunnah form. Scholars explain that the minimum is less: the intention, and water reaching the whole body, with the schools differing on whether rinsing the mouth and nose belongs to that minimum. So yes, a shower can be a ghusl. What turns it into one is the intention and the care that no part is skipped.
screen: `GHUSL REACHES THE WHOLE BODY.` · `REQUIRED: AFTER INTIMACY, AFTER BLEEDING.` · `RECOMMENDED: BEFORE FRIDAY AND EID.` · `AISHAH'S DESCRIPTION, STEP BY STEP.` · then, large: `AND IF YE ARE UNCLEAN, PURIFY YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Walk through the steps without water, slowly enough that you'd notice a missed spot: your hands washed, then the wudu limb by limb, fingers through the roots of your hair, water poured over your head, then running over your shoulders and back, down to your feet, right side, then left. If you make ghusl, you can carry this order into your next one.
Ghusl. The full bath: required after intimacy and after menstruation, recommended before Friday and Eid, done with intention and nothing left dry. Today's word.
Your line: the whole body clean. An ordinary shower can hold more than it seems. Rest well.

1077.title: When there's no water
1077.hook: a clean earth or dust wipe of face and hands replaces washing (5:6)
1077.howItsDone: When Muslims have no water, or water would harm them through illness, they make tayammum: they strike clean earth or dust with their hands and wipe the face and hands, then pray; it stands in for both wudu and ghusl until water is available.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghusl: the whole body clean. Both washings need water. What if there isn't any?

A necklace goes missing in the desert. Aishah has lost it on a journey, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops the caravan to look for it. But the place they've stopped has no water, and they're carrying none. The prayer time comes. People go to Aishah's father, Abu Bakr, and complain: look what she's done. Abu Bakr comes and scolds her, while the Prophet ﷺ sleeps with his head on her lap. Then a verse comes down. And when they finally move her camel, there's the necklace, lying underneath it. Sahih al-Bukhari tells it, at number 334.
screen: `A NECKLACE LOST IN THE DESERT.` → `NO WATER, AND THE PRAYER TIME COMES.` → `A VERSE, AND THE NECKLACE UNDER THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Year one met the word tayammum; today, its story and its steps. The verse is the end of 5:6, the same verse that gave wudu and ghusl. It says that if you are sick, or on a journey, or have come from relieving yourself or been intimate, and you find no water, then go to clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it. Then, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah would not place a burden on you, but He would purify you." That's the spirit of the ruling. The water ran out, and the prayer didn't. In the story, a companion named Usayd ibn Hudayr said this wasn't the first blessing to come through Abu Bakr's family: a lost necklace became an easing for everyone after. How is it done? In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 338, a companion, Ammar ibn Yasir, needed a full bath on a journey with no water. He didn't know about tayammum yet, so he rolled in the dust like an animal, and prayed. When he told the Prophet ﷺ, he was shown something much simpler: strike the earth with your hands, blow on them, wipe your face and your hands. The schools differ on details, one strike or two, the hands to the wrist or further, but the shape is the same, and it stands in for wudu and ghusl alike. In Bukhari 335, the Prophet ﷺ says the earth has been made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification. Water, when there is water. Clean earth, when there isn't.

segments.voice: Rest your palms flat on whatever is beneath you and feel how ordinary that surface is. Slowly lift your hands and, in your mind, wipe your face with them once, then wipe the back of one hand with the other, and switch: that's the shape of tayammum. If you don't pray, sit with the idea in it: when the usual way is closed, there's still a way.
Tayammum. The dry purification: clean earth, the face and the hands, in place of water when there's none or it would harm you. Today's word.
Your line: the earth is clean. Even dust can be a way in. See you tomorrow, at the call.

1078.title: The adhan's words
1078.hook: Allah is greatest, I testify, come to prayer, come to success, then the same at the start
1078.howItsDone: A muezzin calls the adhan when each prayer time begins, from the mosque or over a speaker, and the hadith teaches those who hear it to repeat the phrases after him, answering the two invitations with la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tayammum: the earth is clean. This week, getting ready: conditions, wudu, its breakers, ghusl, tayammum. Today, the call all that readiness answers.

Come to success. Of everything a voice could shout from a rooftop at dawn, that's an odd choice. Not come to duty. Not come, or else. Come to success, hayya ala al-falah, called out over the street at each prayer time, to anyone within earshot. A delivery driver hears it at a red light. A student hears it through a dorm window. A grandmother hears it from a phone app in the kitchen. The whole call is a handful of short phrases.
screen: `COME TO SUCCESS, FROM A ROOFTOP.` → `A DRIVER, A STUDENT, A GRANDMOTHER.` → `THE WORDS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Year three heard the adhan sound across Africa; today, its words in order. Sunan Abu Dawud, number 499, records them as a companion, Abdullah ibn Zayd, received them. It opens: Allahu akbar, Allah is greatest. Then the two testimonies: ashhadu an la ilaha illallah, I testify there is no god but Allah; ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah, I testify that Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. Then two invitations. Hayya ala as-salah, come to prayer. Hayya ala al-falah, come to success. And it closes the way it began: Allahu akbar, and la ilaha illallah. Notice the ring. The call starts with God's greatness and the testimony, swings out to the listener with two invitations, and comes home to the same words. For the dawn call, Sunan Abu Dawud, number 500, adds a line after the invitations: as-salatu khayrun min an-nawm, prayer is better than sleep. And this path has heard how Shia Muslims add their own lines. The listener has a part, too. In Sahih Muslim, number 385, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches that when you hear the call you repeat each phrase after the caller, but at come to prayer and come to success you answer la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah: there is no power and no strength except with God. You're invited to success, and you answer that you can't get there on your own strength. The Qur'an names the call too, in Pickthall's translation: "When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah."
screen: `IT OPENS: ALLAH IS GREATEST.` · `TWO TESTIMONIES, TWO INVITATIONS.` · `IT CLOSES THE WAY IT BEGAN.` · `THE LISTENER ANSWERS: NO POWER BUT WITH GOD.` · then, large: `HAYYA ALA AL-FALAH. COME TO SUCCESS.`

Then go back to the two invitations and stay there: come to prayer, come to success. If you pray, practice the answer, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah; if not, notice what the call names as success.
The adhan's words. Greatness, two testimonies, two invitations, and greatness and testimony again, a call shaped like a ring. Today's word.
Your line: come to success. And the answer: not on my own strength. Tomorrow, the iqamah.
